items.title: UX Mini Challenge 1: Heuristic analysis workshop on user profiles
items.brief:
Objective

The aim of this interactive activity is to practically apply Nielsen's 10 heuristics through a focused evaluation of User Profile sections on various websites. Working in small groups, you'll analyze, discuss, and suggest improvements. You will write up a short report at the end.

Duration

Approximately 60 minutes.

Steps

  1. Look up your group assignment and find a spot to sit together.
    • It is okay if not all group members are present, you can still do the activity.
    • Please indicate only group members present in your peer review.
  2. Each group gets assigned a website with a User Profile/Account Management section.
    • This is different from your Assignment 1 website.
  3. Groups navigate to their website's User Profile section and spend a few minutes exploring the website. (5 mins)
    • Create an account if you need to.
    • If the website does not have a user profile function or requires any kind of payment/info to register, please reach out to your TA or instructor, and we will assign you a different website.
  4. Share your initial impressions within the group. (3 mins)
  5. Conduct a heuristic analysis (20-30 mins)
    • Navigate through the User Profile section
    • Jot down your observations on sticky notes or in Miro.
    • Each group member focuses on two of Nielsen's 10 heuristics.
      1. Visibility of System Status
      2. Match between System and the Real World
      3. User Control and Freedom
      4. Consistency and Standards
      5. Error Prevention
      6. Recognition Rather Than Recall
      7. Flexibility and Efficiency of Use
      8. Aesthetic and Minimalist Design
      9. Recognize, Diagnose, and Recover from Errors
      10. Help and Documentation
  6. Group Discussion (10 mins)
    • Share findings within the group.
    • As a group, use sticky notes or Miro to categorize observations under each heuristic.
  7. Prioritize Issues (5 mins)
    • Use a simple voting system with sticky notes to highlight the top 5 issues.
  8. Recommendation Roundtable (7 mins)
    • Discuss potential improvements for these prioritized issues.
    • Each member suggests one actionable recommendation for one of the top issues.
  9. Submit the report document as PDF to Learn (5 mins)
    • Everyone individually complete the peer review quiz (10% of the score)
      • This quiz is anonymous and only the instructional staff can see it
      • You will receive a maximum of 90% unless all peer reviews from your group clearly indicate that you have done an exceptional job.
    • As a group, submit a PDF file to the dropbox including:
      • List of top 5 prioritized issues and corresponding heuristics
      • Up to three actionable recommendations for how to fix each issue
        • One from each member
  10. Tips for Success
  • Collaboration is key; each heuristic can reveal different issues when viewed from diverse perspectives.
  • Be as specific as possible in your observations and recommendations to make them actionable.

Week 5 · Important guidelines for testing

When approaching a potential participant, say…

We are U of Waterloo students. I’m working on a design project about [your topic]. I’m wondering if you can share some thoughts about the topic and provide some feedback about our prototype to inform our design decisions for our school project.

Our objective for using research methods is a professional skill development activity and to apply existing knowledge derived from classroom learning.
  • Do not use [client's] logo or any related branding in your studies.

items.title: Assignment 1: Heuristic analysis of shopping cart functionality
items.brief:
Objective

Your mission is to conduct a focused heuristic analysis using Nielsen's 10 heuristics on the shopping cart functionality of an existing, popular website. This exercise will equip you with a systematic approach to identify and articulate usability issues.

Scope

  • You will be randomly assigned one popular website with an active shopping cart functionality of the following websites: Amazon, eBay, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Macy's, Zara, Nike, IKEA, Home Depot, Sephora, ASOS, Wayfair, Alibaba, Etsy, H&M, Nordstrom, Costco, Gap, J.Crew, Adidas, Staples, Dell, Overstock, Zappos, QVC, Kohl's, Newegg, Chewy, Saks Fifth Avenue, Uniqlo, Lululemon, Ulta Beauty, Shutterfly, Vistaprint, Forever 21, B&H Photo, Office Depot, the Microsoft Store, T.J.Maxx, the Apple Store, Urban Outfitters, Bose, Lowe's, Hollister, Crate & Barrel, Ticketmaster, REI, Bed Bath & Beyond, Victoria's Secret, Walgreens, The Body Shop, Bath & Body Works, GameStop, AutoZone, Skechers, Dick's Sporting Goods, Marks & Spencer, Swarovski, and Bloomingdale's.
  • Your heuristic analysis should focus solely on the shopping cart experience, from adding items to the cart to the initiation of the checkout process.

Deliverables

  • A 1000-words maximum report (submitted as PDF on Learn).

Heuristic Analysis Report:

  • Introduction: Briefly describe the website, its intended audience, and the specific focus on shopping cart functionality (50 words max).
  • Methodology: Explain very briefly that you will be using Nielsen's 10 heuristics as the framework for your analysis (50 words max).
  • Findings: Use each of Nielsen's 10 heuristics as a subsection to discuss the specific usability issues related to the heuristics found in the shopping cart functionality. Include screenshots for illustration (500 words).
    • In the case you really cannot identify issues on any of the 10, write about where you found the website doing well.
  • Recommendations: For each heuristic, suggest actionable improvements based on your findings (400 words).
  • Appendix (Optional):
    • Include any supplementary material like annotated screenshots (recommend using Snipping Tool, Skitch, Mac default, CleanShot X (Mac), Xnapper, etc.) that you may have used for your analysis.
    • Please review the syllabus on our policy on AI-generated content should you choose to use AI tools to help you complete this assignment.

Grading Criteria

  • Depth of Analysis: 40%
  • Clarity of Communication: 30%
  • Relevance of Recommendations: 30%

Website Assignment

Important: Please inform the TA as soon as you can if your assigned website requires you to reveal information you are uncomfortable with to proceed with the shopping cart. This includes: asking for a phone number, credit card info, or paid membership to sign up. Please complete this step as soon as possible to avoid last-minute issues, this will not be a valid reason to miss the deadline. You should complete the heuristic evaluation way before the submission deadline to allow sufficient time for writing.

items.title: Assignment 2: Contextual inquiry
items.brief:
For your second assignment, you will begin to look at the world with “researcher’s eyes,” reflecting on the things with which you interact, and the quality of that interaction (carry a small notebook around with you and observe and record where you can in addition to this exercise).

For this assignment, do the following contextual inquiry:

  1. Go to a local Cafe of your choice (Livery Yard, Balzac’s, Revel, Coffee Culture, Starbucks, Tim Hortons, Williams Fresh Cafe, etc.) and carry out a one-hour observation.
    • No you cannot go to a restaurant. A restaurant is in a different context from a coffee shop, and it will be difficult to evaluate your work with the same standard as the rest of the class.
  2. Observe and record movements, interactions, sights, sounds, spatial arrangements, and anything else that strikes you. Be an observer only -- it should be the sort of place where you can sit and take notes without bothering anyone. For this exercise, take two pictures of the location/environment you have chosen. You can use audio or video recording as an aid. You should take notes of what is happening in that location for about an hour.
    • Record the time you were there.
    • Observe when it was the busiest during the time you were there.
    • Ideally, use timestamps with your observations.
    • Sketch a quick drawing or overview of the environment.
    • (Optional:) If you have any friends frequenting this location, feel free to interview them about why they go to the location.

  3. Describe (be as detailed as you can) about the setting.
  4. Write down your observations on the spot, then write up longer versions immediately afterward. (Do not interview any strangers. If someone asks you what you are doing, tell them that it’s an assignment in a course about UX research.)
  5. You should spend at least twice as long writing up field notes as you did observe, probably longer. You will be surprised at the amount of detail you can record in one hour.

Your field notes should be a maximum of 1,500 words including:

  • Your first name and last name, obviously;
  • The type of setting, and the date and time of your observations;
  • Why you chose this setting;
  • A rough map and detailed description of the setting (a verbal "snapshot");
  • A description of what you saw; and finally,
  • Your interpretations of what you saw.

The description should be who, what, when, where -- and under a separate heading you can add your assumptions/inferences, and the assumed why, although be careful about too many too-detailed explanations of motivations because they are not part of your contextual inquiry. Conclude with a brief interpretation of at least one organizing principle of the setting. For instance:

  • What patterns do you see?
  • What deviations from the general order do you see?
  • Are some people acting differently or being treated differently than others?

The purpose of the exercise is to get you started in observing and notetaking and to give you the experience of being a “passive” (non-participant) observer in a contextual inquiry.

What are you handing in on Learn?

Upload your assignment as a PDF document in Learn. Your write-up should be no more than 1500 words. For your reference, a rubric has been created which we will use as the basis for grading.

items.title: Group final project: comprehensive UX design for a real-world application
items.brief:
In your final groups of 4-5 people, you will do design work resulting in 3 deliverables at the end of the course that will develop your understanding and abilities to design user experiences. The deliverables must clearly convey practical solutions to the assigned design briefs. As this is a group assignment, you will need to manage your group to complete the assignment (consider signing a group contract; I've attached a template here).​

Your job is to (1) carry out user research to discover if there is a user need for products like the ones mentioned in the design briefs. You will then (2) identify the key user groups, (3) identify the key tasks, (4) set usability goals, (5) develop a prototype and (6) run user research before iterating on the UX design.

Your deliverables will not be graded so much on the quality of your design solution as much as your ability to clearly convey your design ideas in a way that invites feedback, illustrates the potential user experience, and sparks new thinking and discussion of design ideas. We will evaluate your project progress in the following three deliverables:

1a. Pitch Presentation (10%) [Slides due November 12 11:59 pm EST]

This is a product pitch to convey your initial need for the product and key user groups, as well as presenting an overview of your solution (prototype). Think of this as a concise product pitch that you might use in seeking an investor for your design, which likely does not yet exist in more than a concept or rough mock-up. The initial pitch will be presented in class.

Carry out a user research investigation first. Speak with a minimum of 5 users of different systems to the system that you have chosen (e.g., from a competing product or a product in a similar niche). For the design brief, it should not be difficult for you to find users: even friends and family. You should be able to source people who those products are aimed at. They have been chosen so that they are broad in their user base. The pitch will be exactly 3 minutes long, with 2 minutes reserved for questions (5 minutes total). You need to be able to articulate the important parts of your presentation to us in a meaningful way, thus, all materials must be submitted to LEARN the day before class.

You will need to answer the following questions in your pitch presentation:

Is there a need for this system?

  • If not, how can you change it so that it meets a need?
  • Who are the main user groups? There should be more than one user group: what are they?
  • What day-to-day activities do they engage in that are related to the product?
  • What do they do now that is related to that product? Go out and observe them; go out into the real world, where they do this activity now.
  • What is the workflow (the sequence of their activities)? Write this down. You need to observe people, not just interview them. Interview them as well, ask them some questions, but as mentioned when talking about contextual inquiry and field visits, interviewing is a component, but user research is also strongly about observation. Do not overthink this step, overplan it, and spend ages at it. You could do the research phase of this activity easily in a day. Maybe even half a day. The quicker you get your feet wet and jump in, the easier you will find it to come up with hypotheses to test.

Who are the key users for this system?

  • Document all the different user groups you can think of (not too many). Give each group of users a name. Then write down why they need to use the thing you are developing. Remember to think of this from the user’s perspective. Do not write down the functions they will use, but instead think of the goals that they are trying to accomplish. Think of the problem that you are solving for this user.
  • Think about the kind of information that the user needs to achieve those goals. This is where you can start to think about possible functions or features, they may need.
  • After this, write down how you think the groups differ from each other. What is it that makes that group a group? What is it that binds them together?

1b. Prototype [due November 12 11:59 pm EST]

For this assignment, you will be creating a prototype deliverable using Figma. The goal is to design 6 medium-fidelity screens that address a specific customer pain point mentioned in the pitch presentation.

Here are the requirements for the prototype deliverable:

  • Design 6 medium-fidelity screens: Each screen should address the customer pain point and be a functional whole to support user testing. Do not include a login or user profile as part of these screens.
  • Ensure all interactive elements are linked: Make sure that all interactive elements within the screens are properly linked. This will allow users to navigate through the prototype and reach a logical conclusion.
  • Provide a view-only link to the Figma document: Once you have completed the prototype, share a view-only link to the Figma document with all instructors of the class (their email addresses). Please ensure that all instructors can access the document using the provided link. If any instructor cannot view the document, it may result in a loss of marks. If you prefer, you can make the Figma document public.
  • Upload a PDF document showcasing the connections: Additionally, please create a PDF document showcasing the connections between the elements in your prototype. You can use screenshots if necessary. Upload this PDF document to the Dropbox.

If you have any questions or need further clarification, feel free to reach out to us.

2. Final Presentation (10%) [Slides due December 3 11:59 pm EST]

Your final presentation should be ~8 minutes and 2 minutes of Q&A from the class. Similar to the pitch presentation, we will cut you off at the 8-minute mark.

A rough outline for the final presentation (below is required), and you can always choose to add more if you feel it is needed (see rubric as well).

Research Question
Problem Space
Competitor Analysis
Business aspect, how do you make money?
User Research
Prototype (and how it has changed or iterated)
Quick demo of prototype/walkthrough
Lessons learned/challenges
Improvements and next steps

3. Final Report (20%) [due December 4 11:59 pm EST]

Please present a professionally formatted final report that lays out the following:

  1. A write-up of the prototype, along with any changes from the original pitch that you thought necessary while building the prototype
  2. Detailed report on your testing, which includes as a minimum:

a. Introduction

In the final report, you will be presenting a professionally formatted document that provides a comprehensive overview of your UX research project. The report should include detailed information about the prototype, testing process, results, and interpretation of the findings. Additionally, you will need to outline the changes made to the prototype based on the user testing results. You must justify these changes.

b. Prototype Description

Begin the report by providing a thorough write-up of the prototype you developed. Explain the purpose of the prototype and highlight any changes you made from the original pitch presentation. Discuss the specific customer pain point that the prototype aims to address and how the design decisions align with this objective.

c. Testing Process

Describe the setup and apparatus used for testing the prototype. Provide information about the participants involved in the testing phase, including relevant demographics and any recruitment criteria. Explain the testing process itself, including the tasks assigned to participants and any specific instructions provided.

d. Results and Interpretation

Present the results of your user testing in a clear and organized manner. Include both qualitative and quantitative data, highlighting key findings and trends that emerged from the testing sessions. Interpret the results by providing insights and analysis based on the data collected. Discuss any unexpected findings or notable observations that may have influenced the design decisions.

e. Changes to the Prototype

Create a table that outlines the changes needed to address each finding from the user testing. The table should be structured to clearly link each finding with the corresponding design modification. Ensure that the changes address the specific pain points identified during testing and align with best practices in UX design. Note that a minimum of fifteen nuanced and thoughtful findings are expected per prototype.

f. Conclusion

Conclude the report by summarizing the main findings and insights obtained from the UX research process. Reflect on the overall success of the prototype in addressing the customer pain point and meeting the project objectives. Discuss any limitations or challenges encountered during the research and testing phases. Provide recommendations for future iterations or improvements based on the findings and insights from the UX research. Highlight areas that could be further explored or enhanced to optimize the user experience and address any remaining pain points that you were not able to address.

Note: For each prototype, we require a minimum of fifteen findings. Please note that these findings should not be "basic heuristics" as we will deduct marks if your initial design does not meet Nielsen's 10 heuristics. It is crucial that the findings are nuanced, thoughtful, and based on user research.

items.title: Final paper
items.brief:
Your report should contain the following sections, as outlined:

Abstract: a concise, clear, and concise summary of the paper.

Introduction: Describe why the problem you address is important. State what is lacking in the current knowledge and why this research is necessary. State the research question and the objectives of your study. Required: Pick a good problem. This will heavily determine your mark.

Related Works: Provide the necessary background or related work. Synthesize information from a variety of significant sources related to the major point of the paper. Identify any gaps and unresolved questions in existing research and tie them to how your proposed research will address them. Cite all of your sources using any citation format. Required: You must provide a minimum of 5 related peer-reviewed papers to your topic.

Methodology: Provide a detailed description of your proposed research design (e.g., study procedure, how many participants, obtaining consent; how will the researcher(s) interact with the participants), the UX methods that you are planning to use (data collection and analysis), and why those methods are appropriate (i.e., why did you select those methods? Why are they particularly good for addressing your research question?). You should demonstrate that you have a clear understanding of the research methods that you plan to use. Required: The methodology you select must adhere to and address your problem space.

Paper length: approximately 1500-1800 words, or around 5 - 6 pages , excluding the title page and references.

Visual material: Include at least one image, figure, or table in your paper. The visual material should be informative and support the textual information in the paper. For example, you could include a graph that depicts a trend, a table of statistics, or an image relating to your research topic.

Grading: The assignment is out of 80 marks.

  • Abstract (5 marks): Complete, clear, well-organized summary of the 1) topic/research question, 2) research objectives, 3) methodology, and 4) anticipated outcomes/impact of the research. The abstract highlights key points of the research proposal.
  • Introduction (20 marks): The student clearly stated why the research topic/question is important and why this research is necessary. The research question and the objectives of the study are clear and well-defined. A great problem is identified.
  • Background (20 marks): A comprehensive background is provided. The student demonstrates a clear understanding of the importance of the topic and how it relates to other work. Incorporates relevant external sources.
  • Methodology (30 marks): A detailed description of the proposed research design, including study procedure, participants, data collection, and analysis methods. The student demonstrates a clear understanding of the UX methods proposed in the research design and why they are appropriate.
  • Visual material (5 marks): There is at least one image, figure or table. The visual data is presented in an informative, accurate, and creative manner.

What are you handing in on Learn?

Upload your assignment as a PDF document: Final paper Dropbox.

Your submission can be in any format as long as it's consistent and follows Policy 71 adherence (and, of course, exportable as a PDF file).
For the students who want a paper template in .docx file, feel free to use: https://www.acm.org/binaries/content/assets/publications/taps/acm_submission_template.docx.

If you prefer Latex rather than Word, here's the official version: https://www.overleaf.com/latex/templates/acm-conference-proceedings-primary-article-template/wbvnghjbzwpc.

Questions?

Feel free to ask your TAs, [names], if you have any questions regarding this final paper's details. Any questions regarding marks or regrading should be addressed by the instructor, Ali.

items.title: Video proposal: digital product/service
items.brief:
• What is it? Proposal for the term project
  • Specs: A two-minute selfie-style video. Submit copy to the dropbox and supply a link to the video hosted on a streaming service, e.g., YouTube or Vimeo. The video must not be longer than 2 minutes: we will stop watching. Resubmissions must be submitted within 48 hours of initial rejection
  • Due: Friday, 14 January, 18:00 (dropbox)
  • Value: 5% of mark, or 2.5% if it undergoes rejection/resubmission (rubric)

As your design prompt, GBDA 402 is using "Reduced Inequalities within an Among Countries", one of the UN's Sustainable Development Goals. This is a broad topic that gives you a lot of leeway to create a product that your team can plan, design, launch, and test by the end of term.

What Do I Need To Do?

Individuals must create a selfie-style video making a realistic, viable proposal for a digital product / service related to the design prompt. These are subject to approval by the instructors. If your proposal is rejected, you may resubmit a revised proposal within 48 hours; if that is accepted, you will receive partial credit.

Proposals and Teams

Teams must have a minimum of two approved proposals to be approved. This is so you have a back-up option in case your first idea turns out to be too problematic.

• What is this? Requirements for creating your teams
  • Format: Contract in Word document format (template)

To form successfully, teams must have a minimum of two approved proposals. This is so you have a back-up option in case your first idea turns out to be too problematic. Joining a team is up to you: it is not the instructor's responsibility. Individuals who fail to join teams by the deadline have 5% deducted from their final mark.

Aim for a minimum seven people in your teams to have sufficient coverage and assistance for your roles (Product Manager, UX Researcher, Visual Designer, and Business/Marketing Analyst). Team members must fill out the Charter / Working Agreement and submit it to the appropriate dropbox—the due-date is at the top of this document. Take this document seriously: it acts as your contract with one another, and helps you in times of conflict. All team members must append their signatures to the document, or at least type their names as Indications of agreement. The document covers the following:

Basics

  • Team Name. Provide a team name, or we'll give you a truly cringey name
  • Team Members. Provide name, ID, email, and phone number
  • Team Roles. Suggested roles: Product Manager, UX Researcher, Visual Designer, and Business/Marketing Analyst. Provide name, role, and responsibilities

  • Preliminary. Provide name and individual strengths, weaknesses, and values. Understanding these helps create a more balanced, robust team.
  • Conduct. Based upon your listed values, how will you conduct yourselves? Be specific.
  • Work Process. How will you manage the deliverable process so that you meet your deadlines? Be specific.
  • Conflict Resolution. What do you plan to do should members come into conflict, or if members do not abide by the charter? Be specific.

  • Daily Check-Ins. How will they occur? What is the extent/depth?
  • Mobile Phones/Headphones. What is appropriate usage, especially in meetings?
  • Definition of ‘Done’. When is a prototype ready to test? When is a deliverable ready to submit to the dropbox? How do you expect reports to be organised/formatted?
  • Team Member Contribution and Output. What is the procedure for the team to decide priorities and set goals? What types of decisions can be made without the whole team’s input?
  • Meetings. How often will you meet? Where/When/How long?
  • Decisions re: Missing Meetings. If a member misses a meeting, do they agree by default to the decisions made by the team members who attended the meeting?
  • Break Times. When will break decisions be made? How will you take a break? When? How long will the break last? (You’ll refer to this more often than you expect)

items.title: Tips and tricks for leading group discussions
items.brief:
Your role is to lead your class to help get to a shared understanding of parts of the paper you read. While you may answer a few questions from your classmates, the goal of this time is to discuss specific aspects of the paper.

Focus Management:

  1. Ensure you start off with a focus.
    1. You can pick a focus on reading the paper.
    2. If you don’t have a focus, you could either talk about the core contribution of the paper (answer questions about why the community cares about this paper, or why we are making you read this paper), how your classmates would use the output of this paper in their studies or the impact of the paper in the HCI community long term.
  2. Work towards an output – ensure that you communicate this with the team at the beginning and during the discussion.

Participant Management:

  1. Encourage people to speak – diverse perspectives make for a better discussion
  2. No one person should be talking for more than 2 minutes
  3. Ensure that participants do not paraphrase someone else’s comments as their own

Personal Management:

  1. Know your content – and be willing to learn from others
  2. Everyone has their own leadership style, use this time to understand what you’re comfortable with:
    1. Are you ok telling participants to pause?
    2. Are you an active or a passive leader?
    3. Do you prefer the gentle nudge, or a more direct approach?
  3. Think through how you would like to conduct your meeting before it starts, remember the discussion is as important as your presentation
